_comment: Presentation. ALL of it is TUNABLE and none of it is a mechanic. The expected feedback is 'too dark', 'the grass is the wrong green', 'the creatures don't move enough' — every one of those has to be answerable by editing this file rather than by editing a scene.
_comment_scale: Nothing here sets a collider or a hit range. Art is fitted to the gameplay size the species and the controller already declare; if a value in this file could change how far an attack reaches, it is in the wrong file.

trainer._comment_height: Metres, matched to the CharacterBody3D capsule in scenes/player/player.tscn. The model is measured and scaled to this, so a replacement of any size drops in without touching the scene.
trainer._comment_yaw: Degrees of correction for which way the source model faces. Verified from a survey frame, not assumed — there is no convention across asset packs.
trainer._comment_clips: Five clips, authored by tools/art_pipeline/blender/animate_humanoid.py and baked into the .glb, so the role and the clip name are the same string and nothing is retargeted. MQ1A rebuilt them as key-pose authored cycles (contact/loading/mid-stance/toe-off/whip/mid-swing/reach through a cyclic spline, on render-verified bone axes) with pelvis rotation, chest counter-rotation and head stabilisation.
trainer._comment_tool_swing: OP21-24. The chop clip's own length and the frame the axe is IN the wood, in clip fractions. tool_hold.gd reads these so the gather resolves on the impact pose rather than at an arbitrary half-way point, and so the swing state holds for exactly as long as the clip plays instead of cutting to idle mid-arc. Re-derive both from animate_humanoid.py's author_chop() (15 frames at 24 fps; impact keyed at frame 9) if that clip is re-timed. TUNABLE.
trainer._comment_gait_speeds: OF5, TUNABLE. Metres per second each gait clip was AUTHORED for — animate_humanoid.py derives the cycle length and stride from these so a planted foot sweeps back under the body at the same speed the controller drives it. trainer_model.gd scales playback by actual ground speed / this value (clamped 0.5-1.4x in character_model.gd), so cadence stays honest through acceleration, slopes and any movement.json retune. If locomotion speeds are retuned by more than the clamp covers, re-bake the clips against the new numbers rather than widening the clamp: past ~1.4x a gait reads as frantic, not fast.
trainer._comment_libraries: Empty now, and kept as a key because the merge path still works. KayKit's Ranger needed it: that character ships a rig with zero clips and the motion in shared libraries. This model carries its own clips. Its skeleton is also NOT KayKit's — KayKit's character is about two heads tall and sheet 04's trainer is 6.25, so neither the weights nor the clips transfer between them.
trainer._comment_model: Sheet 04's trainer, produced through tools/art_pipeline. The body and the head were generated separately and grafted: nine whole-figure candidates across three rounds all came back with a blank ovoid for a face, because at a 30k budget spread over a standing figure an eye socket is smaller than the triangles available to describe it.

sky._comment: Mid-morning, high summer, clear. Taken from the key art board rather than invented: a warm low-contrast sky over saturated grass is most of what makes the reference read as inviting rather than as a tech demo.
sky._comment_horizon_colour_b12: B12 aerial perspective. #b9c8cf -> #b7ccc3 (H154 S10% V80). Distance was greying toward blue-grey (H199) with no hue rotation, while the key art's far hills shift to a desaturated cool green (H116, S12%); this value is roughly halfway between the two. FOG-ONLY change: no sun property, energy or colour touched. CRITICAL -- this MUST stay identical to environment.fog_colour below (see the EV8 comment on that key): fog_sky_affect is 0, so fog colour and horizon colour are the only two things that make distant terrain fade into the sky without a seam.
sky._comment_horizon_colour_vp1_seam: VP1 sky retune round 1. Was #d3cebd (T1-HALL-4's warm tan, H43 S24% V83), landed to fix a DIFFERENT seam against the OLD fog colour. A terrain-lane finding on this same branch: `terrain_playground.json`'s `shader.aerial_fade_colour` (the ground's own distance fade) is `#aebcc4`, a cool blue-grey (H204 S12% V77) -- about 160 degrees of hue away from the warm tan sky/fog, so distant terrain now cooled toward blue-grey right up against a warm tan band at the horizon: a new seam, same failure mode T1-HALL-4's own comment warns about, just with the ground and sky on opposite sides of it this time. #b4c8cc (H190 S12% V80) sits between the two -- close to the ground fade's saturation and value, hue nudged back from 204 toward neutral so it still reads as a lit sky rather than the ground's own colour repeated overhead. `ground_horizon_colour` (#b9c8cf) was ALREADY close to the ground fade and needed no change. environment.fog_colour below moves with this value, per the CRITICAL note two lines up.
sky._comment_clouds: SKY-CLOUDS. `cloud_coverage` above 0 swaps the ProceduralSkyMaterial for shaders/sky_clouds.gdshader; 0 falls back to the gradient below, which the shader reproduces exactly so turning clouds off lands on the sky they replaced rather than a different one. This exists because four blind passes in a row named the empty sky: measured horizontal variation 0.020 against 0.140-0.289 across the Palworld references, per-channel standard deviation of 2-8 (a pure gradient), 30-50% of the wide frames carrying no information at all, against cumulus in every keyart panel, both meadow reference frames and four of five Palworld shots. world_look.gd::_apply_sky already argued the case and proposed an HDRI panorama; a generated sky is the better fit for the same slot -- no asset to source or license, it drifts on the wind, and each time of day drives it with one number. `coverage` is the knob that matters: 0.35-0.6 is the interesting range, above that is overcast. TUNABLE per time of day.
sky._comment_cloud_form: SKY-CLOUDS round 2. A blind pass with the first numbers in frame called the sky `a flat gradient with two or three blurred cloud smudges pasted in with no form and no sun cue`, and it was right: at coverage 0.46 with scale 1.35 the projected noise put one or two very large, very soft features across the whole dome. More coverage, a harder density ramp and a smaller projection scale give banks with edges instead of smudges.
sky._comment_cloud_form_vp1_retune: VP1 sky retune round 1. The judge's new complaint is the opposite failure from round 2's: `cloud_coverage` had crept back up to 0.5 and `cloud_scale` to 1.5 across later passes, and together they now read as 'mackerel / overcast -- a busy stipple across the whole dome instead of a few large cumulus'. `scale` is a frequency multiplier on the noise coordinate (`plane = dir.xz * t * scale` in the shader): a LARGER number packs more noise cells into the same patch of sky, i.e. SMALLER, more numerous features on screen, and a smaller number stretches the same cells wider, i.e. FEWER, LARGER ones. So the fix for 'a few large cumulus' is a SMALLER `scale`, same direction as this round's target number: 1.5 -> 0.9. `coverage` moved down with it (0.5 -> 0.4, `t0 = 1-coverage` is the density threshold) so fewer cells clear the threshold at all, instead of a lower-frequency field still covering half the dome.
sky._comment_sun_disc_t1_sky: T1-SKY. shaders/sky_clouds.gdshader's own sun_size/sun_glow uniforms default to 0.022/0.35 (a blown, hard-edged disc with a near-invisible glow term -- glow decays as pow(sun_dot,24) so at these raw defaults it reads as a second, even tighter disc rather than a soft halo). T1-LIGHT's 2026-08-29 fix set small tuned values on the NIGHT preset only (sun_size 0.006/sun_glow 0.05, a subdued moon). Day and golden never set these keys at all, so world_look.gd::_apply_cloud_sky's per-key `if cfg.has(...)` guard never touched the shader parameters for them -- on a freshly created sky material (every fresh scene/tool boot) that left the RAW shader defaults in effect, which is exactly the blown white sticker-disc a blind judge caught in the golden snap (JUDGE-VISUAL-2026-08-29.md subject 7). Sized well below the raw default but well above night's subdued moon -- day gets a normal bright sun, golden's own override (below) goes slightly larger and warmer for the low sunset sun the key art's panel asks for.
sky._comment_sun_disc_edge_vp1: VP1 sky retune round 1. Day never set `sun_disc_edge` before, so it ran at the shader's raw default (0.35 -- 65% of the disc's radius is soft falloff), which the judge called 'a huge soft blob rather than a crisp modest disc'. Set explicitly here, well toward night's crisp moon (0.93) but short of it -- the sun should still have a thin bloom around a real edge, not a razor coin. Paired with a small trim to `sun_size`/`sun_glow` (0.01/0.16 -> 0.009/0.12) so the now-defined edge isn't sitting on an oversized, over-glowing disc. Golden and dawn deliberately do NOT get this key -- see the older `_comment_moon_disc_t1_hall_4` comment under the night preset below: a low sunset/sunrise sun is meant to bloom, and giving it the same crisp edge as a high midday sun would undo that on purpose.
sky._comment_sun_glow_falloff_vis_world: VIS-WORLD. `sun_glow_falloff` is new: shaders/sky_clouds.gdshader's `glow` term used a hardcoded exponent of 24.0, which fixes the halo's angular width no matter what `sun_size`/`sun_disc_edge` (those only shape the crisp `disc`) or `sun_glow` (only scales the halo's brightness) were set to -- that fixed width works out to roughly a 27-degree-diameter halo, about 54x the real sun's size, which several blind passes read as 'a giant white sun blob' rather than a disc with a glow around it. 200.0 narrows that to about a 9.5-degree halo (halo diameter in degrees = 2*acos(2^(-1/exponent))*180/PI) -- still a generous stylised glow, just one that sits around a visible disc instead of swallowing it. `times.golden` below sets its own, wider value; every other time of day inherits this base value since none of them override the key.
sky._comment_panorama: An HDRI panorama, when the time of day names one. The procedural gradient below is the FALLBACK and stays because a missing texture should degrade to the old sky rather than to a black void. The critic measured the procedural sky's horizontal variation at 0.020 against Palworld's 0.140-0.289 and said the build sky 'contributes nothing' — a ProceduralSkyMaterial can make a vertical gradient and a soft sun blob and nothing else, ever. No amount of tuning puts a cloud in it.
sky._comment_panorama_ev8: EV8. day.hdr named here was pulled: a static equirect photo has its OWN baked-in sun position, unrelated to this file's sun.pitch_deg/yaw_deg, so whichever way a viewpoint faces, the photographed sky and the actual DirectionalLight3D can disagree about where the light is coming from. That is exactly what a blind pass caught -- one viewpoint's sky read as dusk while its own ground lit as bright midday, in the same frame, both driven by the same 'day' preset. The procedural gradient has no such seam: its glow is generated from the real sun direction, so it agrees with the ground in every direction, not just the survey's five. Costs the cloud detail the panorama bought; buys back the 'one sky/fog treatment shared everywhere' EV8 exists to deliver. TUNABLE -- naming a panorama here is legitimate again once one exists whose baked sun can be kept in sync, or once multiple panoramas are matched to sun position by heading.
sky._comment_vp1: VP1 (visual parity program, 2026-09-01). Every blind pass since the cloud shader landed named the same defect: 'smeared airbrush blotches in every outdoor frame'. shaders/sky_clouds.gdshader now builds billowed cumulus with a defined edge on a shell projection (large overhead, compressed at the horizon), a cloud BASE colour for the underside, a thin cirrus layer and a horizon haze band that lands on horizon_colour so sky and terrain fog meet in one band. The keys below drive it; every one is set in this BASE block on purpose -- world_look.gd only writes keys the merged config has, so a key missing here would never reach the shader. cloud_lit/cloud_shade/cloud_base/sun_colour are now in world_look.gd's _COLOUR_KEYS so the driven clock lerps them instead of snapping at the midpoint.
sky._comment_cloud_high_opacity_vp1: VP1 sky retune round 1. Was 0.35. The judge named the thin cirrus layer specifically as 'a big part of the mackerel read' -- at 0.35 it is nearly as visible as the cumulus below it, so the whole dome reads as one busy stippled texture instead of a clear layer of large cumulus with a faint high layer above. 0.18 keeps the cirrus present (it is still what stops the sky reading as one flat depth) without competing with the cumulus for attention.
sky._comment_haze_vp1: VP1 sky retune round 1. `horizon_haze_height`/`horizon_haze_strength` were 0.14/0.55 -- the judge: 'the horizon haze washes the bottom of the sky to near-white'. Both cut (0.14->0.10, 0.55->0.35) so the band is present -- it is still what makes the sky and the fogged terrain meet without a hard line -- without flattening a third of the dome to one pale colour. `horizon_haze_colour` is new: see the shader's own comment on the `haze_colour` uniform. Biased bluer than `horizon_colour` (#b4c8cc) rather than reusing it, so the haze band itself reads as atmosphere rather than as a second coat of the same horizon paint.

sun._comment: One directional light. `pitch` well above the horizon so shadows are short and readable under a top-down-ish combat camera; long raking shadows look dramatic in a screenshot and hide the opponent in a fight.
sun._comment_yaw_visual_light: VISUAL-LIGHT. Was -40, which GATE-E-STRONGHOLD-ART's own investigation named exactly: -40 puts the sun in the NORTH sky (world_look.gd rotates the DirectionalLight3D so its light travels FROM the yaw direction TOWARD the opposite one -- verified with a Basis.from_euler probe, sun_dir.z > 0 at -40, i.e. north), while the chapter's whole play direction and the stronghold's hero face (landmark.gd's own comment: 'every approach to this building is on its south side') point SOUTH. Every south-facing surface the player actually walks toward -- not just the stronghold, which only got a local albedo/fire-basket workaround because 'turning the sun around... lives in the environment config another lane owns' -- was backlit at every hour of the chapter. This lane owns that file now. Flipped 180 degrees (-40 -> 140) rather than re-deriving an azimuth from scratch: it is the exact opposite direction, same elevation, so shadow length/readability (this block's own stated reason for the pitch) is untouched, and it is trivially reversible if a specific site turns out to want the sun from a third direction. Sun is now in the south sky; south-facing hero faces are front-lit. GATE-E-STRONGHOLD-ART's castle albedo/fire-basket compensation is stepped back in the same change (building_prefabs.json, landmark.gd) now that the real cause is fixed.
sun._comment_shadow_reach_t1_hall_4: T1-HALL-4, 2026-08-30, JUDGE-6 defects 10 and 12. 220 -> 420. Two of the report's findings are the same missing shadow at two ranges. At golden hour, with a very low sun, "the crenellations cast NO SHADOW DOWN THE PARAPET BELOW THEM. The fortress does not appear to be casting shadows onto itself at all, WHICH IS A LARGE PART OF WHY IT STAYS FLAT IN EVERY DAYLIGHT FRAME" -- and separately, the 400m approach frame has no cast shadow anywhere on the building. 220m was tuned for a player walking a meadow, where nothing past it is worth a shadow map. The Hall broke that assumption: it is 60m of building whose establishing shots are taken from 165m and 400m, so at 220m the SUBJECT of the chapter's three most important frames sat outside the shadow cascade entirely and lit flat. 420 covers the 400m approach stand with margin. The cost is real and is the reason this is not larger: two PSSM splits now spread over 420m instead of 220m, so near-field shadow edges soften. That trade is worth taking here because the near field is already carrying `shadow_normal_bias` 2.0 for its own reasons and because a soft shadow on a tuft is invisible while a missing shadow on the fortress is the judge's finding.
sun._comment_shadow: Normal bias fights the acne that a heightmap terrain produces at grazing angles. Raise it if the ground looks striped; lower it if small props stop casting.
sun._comment_energy: Bright. The first pass at real lighting overshot into gloom: the arena went near-black and the creatures stopped being readable, which is a worse failure than the flat lighting it replaced. Value RANGE was the goal — bright sun, real shadows — not darkness.
sun._comment_pitch_r9_4: R9.4. Was -52. The blind critic found frames 01-04 'effectively flat-lit' -- boosting contrast 3x revealed almost no terrain form -- while frame 05, the only low-sun frame, was 'by a wide margin the best-lit frame in the set' and the only one whose value statistics land inside the references' range. Dropped to -44 rather than to 05's -13: the original comment's reason for a high sun is real (long raking shadows hide the opponent under a top-down-ish combat camera) and this keeps shadows short while giving slopes a lit and a shaded side. TUNABLE, and the thing to re-check first if combat readability regresses.
sun._comment_vp1: VP1: energy 1.35->1.4 and a slightly warmer colour to compensate the terrain macro darkening VP2 adds; shadow_normal_bias 2.0->1.7 for tree-trunk/rock contact (the blind pass: 'every boulder floats with no contact shadow'). Re-check the ground for acne with tools/diag_shadow_bias.gd if it stripes.

environment._comment: Tonemap and fog. ACES holds highlights on sunlit grass instead of clipping them to white, which was the single worst thing about the previous prototype's look.
environment._comment_ambient_cover: Was 1.5. A blind pass measured the darkest 1% of six of twelve frames clipping to literal luminance 0.0, against a Palworld floor near 30/255, while our mean saturation ran 0.53-0.72 against their 0.40-0.47 -- acid green beside holes. Note the tension with the R9.4 note below, which CUT ambient because a critic had measured the darkest 5% at 126, far too bright: this file has oscillated on this number before and the two complaints are about opposite ends of the range. This is a modest step toward the floor, not a return to the R9.4 regime, and the value range is worth re-MEASURING rather than re-arguing next round. TUNABLE.
environment._comment_exposure_ev4_lighting: EV4-textures-lighting. Was 1.22. Three blind-critic rounds on EV4-textures's own path frames independently named a blown-white sunlit path and (separately) an unmotivated dark diagonal band, and it took both diag_shadow_band.gd and diag_slope_check.gd (scratch, not shipped) to separate two different causes hiding under one description. `square-convergence`'s band IS a real occlusion shadow -- confirmed by toggling sun.shadow_enabled off, which removed it -- from the Barn 6m from that viewpoint's camera; raising directional_shadow/size back to 4096 changed nothing (pixel-identical edge), which rules out SA1's atlas cut as the cause. `grandpas-house-route`'s flanking bands are NOT a shadow at all -- identical with shadow_enabled true or false, identical with SSAO on or off, and the ground there measures dead flat (slope_degrees_at = 0.0 across the whole sampled width, confirmed with the heightfield's own function, no scene load needed). That one is pure contrast: ordinary grass at luma ~70-100 sitting next to a path blown to ~190-200 reads as 'a shadow with no caster' even though the grass itself is unremarkable. Fixing the blown highlight therefore addresses both: `near_luma` (tools/frame_stats.py, mean luma of the bottom 15% of frame) measured 0.692 on grandpas-house-route against Palworld's own 0.492-0.600, and the sunlit path itself sampled at ~197/255. A modest exposure trim did almost nothing (1.22 -> 0.95 moved the path 0/255 -- ACES's shoulder is that flat up here); it took a real cut to 0.6 to bring the path to ~151/255, inside the Palworld range. TUNABLE, and the first thing to revisit if 'day' reads dim elsewhere.
environment._comment_ambient_ev4_lighting: EV4-textures-lighting. Was 1.02. The Barn's real shadow measured near-black (luma 10-20/255) at its darkest, well under any reference near-field value -- lifting ambient is the one lever that reaches it without touching the sunlit path much (measured: tripling ambient moved the sunlit path only ~197->215, but moved the shadow floor ~15->40, because ambient is a much larger fraction of what a SHADOWED point receives). Went with a smaller, safer step than that -- 1.02 -> 1.5, not 3x -- because a big ambient increase measurably crept back into the sunlit path too once combined with the exposure cut above (both scale the same HDR value before tonemap), which would have undone the highlight fix. Left the shadow darker than ideal rather than fight that tradeoff further; see the EV4-textures-lighting DONE.md entry for what a blind pass said after this.
environment._comment_fog: Very light, and warm rather than grey. It exists to separate near hills from far ones; at any strength where you notice it as fog, it is too strong.
environment._comment_fog_measured: Halved from 0.0022. At the old density the blind critic measured `03-rise-overlook` at mean saturation 0.235 against 0.51 for a frame in the same biome, and said fog was 'eating the world rather than describing depth' — every object past ~150m a grey stamp. The reference does the same job with comparable haze and keeps a saturated tree band in front of it, so the fix is less fog, not less distance.
environment._comment_fog_colour_ev8: EV8. Was #cdd0c6, which does not match sky.horizon_colour (#b9c8cf) above. fog_sky_affect is 0 on purpose (see below), so the sky is never fogged -- which means the fog colour and the horizon colour are the ONLY two things that have to agree for terrain fading into the distance to meet the sky without a seam. A blind pass caught the mismatch as a hard pale band sitting in the middle of a frame, well short of the true horizon: distant terrain fogs to #cdd0c6 while the sky right above it sits at #b9c8cf, and the two visibly disagree. Matched to horizon_colour exactly.
environment._comment_fog_colour_b12: B12 aerial perspective. #b9c8cf -> #b7ccc3 (H154 S10% V80), rotating the hue distance greys toward -- currently blue-grey (H199) with no hue rotation -- roughly halfway to the key art's far-hill cool green (H116 S12%). FOG-ONLY: no sun property, energy or colour touched; dimming/re-tinting the sun would desaturate every other asset class to rescue the ground instead. CRITICAL, per the EV8 comment directly above: this MUST stay identical to sky.horizon_colour, or the horizon seam that comment describes comes back.
environment._comment_fog_colour_t1_hall_4: T1-HALL-4, 2026-08-30, JUDGE-6 defect 11/10. #b7ccc3 -> #d3cebd, and `sky.horizon_colour` moves with it -- the EV8 comment above is right that these two MUST stay identical and this edit keeps them so. The judge: "there is a desaturated DARK SLATE haze band across the horizon while the sky above it is clear blue and the ground is lit by a WARM SUN. The frames do not agree with themselves about the time of day, and the haze band is dark enough that IT SWALLOWS THE FORTRESS in H-01 and H-02 rather than separating it." Both halves are answered by the same move: the new value is warmer (hue rotated from a cool green-grey toward the sun's own #fff6e6 family) so the distance agrees with the light, and lighter (V80 -> V83) so the band behind the fortress lifts instead of closing on it. That is literally the judge's own prescription for defect 1 -- "push a lighter warm haze behind it so it reads as the dark shape" -- and it is the half of the silhouette fix that does not come out of the building's own albedo. B12's reasoning for rotating toward the key art's far-hill hue still stands; the key art's far hills are warmer than #b7ccc3 read them, which is what this correction is.
environment._comment_fog_colour_vp1_seam: VP1 sky retune round 1, coordination finding from the terrain lane. #d3cebd -> #b4c8cc, and `sky.horizon_colour` moves with it -- see that key's own `_comment_horizon_colour_vp1_seam` above for the full reasoning: `terrain_playground.json`'s `shader.aerial_fade_colour` (the ground's own distance fade) is `#aebcc4`, a cool blue-grey nothing like T1-HALL-4's warm tan, so distant terrain was cooling toward blue-grey right up against a warm cream fog/horizon -- the exact seam failure this file's own EV8/B12 comments warn about, just with the ground on the cool side this time instead of the sky. #b4c8cc reconciles the two without landing exactly on the ground's own colour (which would read as the ground repeated overhead rather than a lit sky).
environment._comment_ambient: Sky ambient with a real colour underneath it. `sky_contribution` blends between the two. Quadrupling ambient energy with pure sky ambient moved the survey frames by NOTHING — sky radiance does not reach the terrain under the Compatibility renderer the harness is forced to use — while an explicit colour lifted the shaded ground by 55%. Specifying both means shaded ground is filled under either renderer, and 'shadows are filled by this much of this colour' is a decision somebody made rather than a side effect of a procedural sky.
environment._comment_ambient_sky_t1_hall_4: T1-HALL-4, 2026-08-30, JUDGE-6 defect 5 -- "about a quarter of the frame is a flat near-black slab ... the keep's shadowed face retains essentially no bounce light and no visible texture. Compare palworld-04's shadowed cliff faces, which keep colour and detail. HERE SHADOW EQUALS BLACK" (measured on the shipped frames at 16.9% of `H-06` below luminance 26), plus the near-black tree in `H-05`. 0.5 -> 0.25, and note carefully that this RAISES fill without touching `ambient_energy`. That distinction is the whole point, because the two live findings pull opposite ways: this defect wants more light in shadow, while `_comment_ambient_cover` above records the last pass raising ambient_energy 1.5 -> 2.1 for the same reason and a different pass cutting it for the opposite one. This file has oscillated on that number twice and a third swing would be the wrong move. `ambient_sky_contribution` is a free lever instead, and `_comment_ambient` directly below says why in its own words: "sky radiance does not reach the terrain under the Compatibility renderer". project.godot ships gl_compatibility (D01), so this is not a harness quirk -- it is the renderer the game runs on. At 0.5, half of the ambient budget was being spent on a sky term that contributes nothing to any frame anyone has ever judged. Moving it to 0.25 hands that half back to the explicit `ambient_colour`, which does reach, so shaded faces gain roughly 1.5x their fill while sunlit surfaces -- where ambient is a small fraction of the total -- barely move. The blown-highlight fix `_comment_exposure_ev4_lighting` bought is therefore not at risk. NOT a claim that ambient occlusion is fixed. `ssao_enabled` below is TRUE and is a no-op: Compatibility does not implement SSAO, so every frame in every judging round has been rendered without it and the key has been decorative since it was written. JUDGE-6's "enable/repair contact shadows and AO globally" cannot be answered from this file under this renderer; what can be answered is the sun-shadow reach above and this fill. Real contact occlusion needs either a renderer change (D01, locked) or baked/geometry contact, and that is named as a remainder in the lane's handover rather than quietly left looking done. ROUND 2, same lane, after rendering: 0.25 was not enough and the number that says so is the one JUDGE-6 raised. Its defect 5 box (H-06, x 900-1280, y 0-620) measured mean L 28.8 with a high-pass texture sd of 4.10 on the judged frames; after this lane's stone value drop it read 19.8 and 2.67 -- DARKER, and with LESS readable texture, which is the defect getting worse rather than better. That is a cost of the silhouette fix and it is this lane's to pay, not to report and leave. 0.25 -> 0.10 hands over almost the whole sky term. Still not `ambient_energy`, for the reason the round-1 note gives: that number has oscillated twice already and this file should stop swinging it.
environment._comment_character_emission_floor: T1-WORLD. How much of character_model.gd's additive emission floor applies at this time of day, 0..1. The floor is a CONSTANT additive lift that keeps a dark-uniformed NPC out of the ACES tonemap's toe; its own comment records it tuned against a daylight frame (day body luma 30.6/35.4) and then checked at night (51.7/59.5), reading that night jump as acceptable. The whole-board night pass shows what it looks like beside something correctly lit: in shots/ground/ground-04-band4-ironwood-night-vista.png the band-4 trainer is the BRIGHTEST object in the frame, fully daylit warm tan against a blue night, while the player two metres away is a correct dark silhouette. A constant additive term cannot be right at more than one light level, because at night everything it competes with has dropped an order of magnitude and it has not. 1.0 here is the base and means unchanged, so every daylight measurement in that comment still holds exactly; night cuts it. TUNABLE -- raise the night value if NPCs stop reading at all after dark, lower it if they still look self-lit. ROUND 3, measured: 0.25 was too far. A blind before/after re-judge counted 59% of the pixels inside the band-4 trainer's torso and legs at exactly (0,0,0), against 0.3% before the change, and frame-wide pure black rising 12.5% -> 19% -- the coat, cape and boots had no material or form left and the silhouette existed only where it occluded grass. That is trading a wrongly-lit figure for a clipped one, which is not a fix. 0.5 keeps the figure off daylight exposure while leaving the outfit some range to read as cloth. The head and hands are a SEPARATE and unrelated defect -- see the T1-WORLD verdict sec5; they are near-white untextured art on the rig, not a lighting term, which is why they stay bright at night no matter what this value is and why the same pale face shows on the village NPCs in frames taken before any of this existed.
environment._comment_adjustment_defaults_t1_sky: T1-SKY. night._comment_night_light:
NIGHT-LIGHT. Was ambient_energy 0.35 / ambient_sky_contribution 0.6 / sun.energy 0.12 / exposure 0.85 -- measured (tools/frame_stats.py on tools/capture_night_light.gd's output) at near_luma 0.000 and value_spread 0.00 across two survey_band2.gd viewpoints: a literal flat black frame, matching three consecutive blind-critic rounds calling night 'crushed to near-total black' and confirming (round 2, camera moved to ~10m) that it was not a framing problem. First fix attempt only cut ambient_sky_contribution and raised ambient_energy/sun.energy by 2-3x, reasoning from world_look.gd's own comment that sky-sourced ambient contributes ZERO under the Compatibility renderer every judged capture uses (D06) -- that IS real, but re-measuring after landing it found near_luma still 0.000, unmoved. A scratch diagnostic (mutated the live Environment directly, not committed) isolated why: shadow_enabled made no difference, but a ~20x ambient_energy jump and, separately, a ~36x sun.energy jump each independently produced a big jump in near_luma from a small one doing nothing -- the signature of ACES's toe (env.tonemap_mode = TONE_MAPPER_ACES in world_look.gd::_apply_environment), which maps a wide range of low linear input to near-zero output by design, so a 2-3x nudge near the bottom of that range is invisible and it takes an order-of-magnitude change to cross it. exposure multiplies the same linear value before the ACES curve and reproduces the same effect without needing absurd raw energies that wash out colour variety (a bare 20x-ambient test read 88% one hue family). Landed on a split between ambient_energy, sun.energy and exposure, each raised well short of day's own values, that crosses the toe without flattening night into a dim day.

Round 2, after a blind visual-judge pass on the round-1 numbers (which DID cross the toe -- near_luma 0.000 -> 0.024-0.139 across the three test frames, real movement): the critic named two new, in-scope defects. (a) The ~94m quarry-overlook viewpoint was still called '70%+ pure black, no ground form at all' -- that viewpoint is simply far enough that ambient/moon fill from round 1 wasn't reaching it; answered here with a further ambient_energy/exposure lift. (b) The ranger-camp-close frame showed 'a hard value seam... reads as a light falloff/attenuation cliff... an artifact,' which is what a near-horizontal light does to gentle terrain undulation: this file's own day-preset comment already rejected a steep-vs-shallow sun pitch tradeoff for exactly this reason ('R9.4... dropped to -44 rather than -13... keeps shadows short'), and round 1's moon sat at an even more grazing -8 than day's rejected -13. Steepened to -20.

Round 3, after a second blind pass on round 2 (near_luma moved again, 0.024-0.139 -> 0.135-0.222, real movement, so round 2 counted too): the critic's own words were 'night doesn't read as night -- it reads as day with the lights off... the ground keeps the same warm tan/olive hues as the day frames, just dimmed.' Round 2 over-corrected on the legibility axis and lost the mood axis -- exactly what this entry's own round-1/2 TUNABLE warning called out in advance ('exposure past roughly 3x... eroding the night-blue cast'). Root cause: physically-multiplied light x albedo has no separate 'this is night' filter the way scotopic human vision desaturates a moonlit scene -- once ambient/exposure are raised enough to reveal the ground, they reveal the terrain's true daytime-green albedo just as faithfully as the sun does. Fixed by adding one: world_look.gd::_apply_environment() now reads `adjustment_enabled`/`adjustment_saturation`/`adjustment_contrast` (Godot's own colour-grade layer, previously never wired to anything) so night can desaturate toward its ambient_colour's blue cast instead of only ever getting brighter. Pulled exposure and ambient_energy back down slightly now that desaturation is doing part of the 'reads as night' work instead of raw brightness alone, pushed ambient_colour further from neutral toward blue, and gave the sky itself a little energy/glow so the upper frame is dark navy rather than the crushed pure-black the critic also named ('no stars, no moon, no ambient gradient at all'). Same critic pass separately flagged a hard-edged shadow on the quarry path as an artifact -- confirmed (by rendering the SAME viewpoint at both times of day) to be present identically in the DAY frame too, so it does not react to time-of-day lighting at all and is not a NIGHT-LIGHT defect; left alone and reported separately, not owned by this preset. TUNABLE -- if this still reads as dim-day rather than night, adjustment_saturation is the next dial, not exposure.

sky._comment_top_colour_vis_world: VIS-WORLD. Night measured sky 0.0% and horizon 0.00 in all five night frames, every round: the sky was indistinguishable from the ground, so there was no horizon at all. That is not a judgement call -- frame_stats.sky_mask classifies sky as blue-band hue with value > 0.35, and #0a1330's value is 0.19, so no night pixel could ever qualify. Raised so the sky sits ABOVE the land in value, which is what a real night looks like and what the key art's night panel does (navy with readable silhouettes). The ground is deliberately NOT raised with it -- see exposure below. TUNABLE.
sky._comment_sun_glow_t1_light: T1-LIGHT. A blind pass on the golden->night BLEND (hour 21, i.e. between this preset and golden, not either keyframe alone) caught a huge blown-out white disc dominating a quarter of the sky -- 'reads as an exposure/bloom bug, not a sunset'. shaders/sky_clouds.gdshader's sun_glow/sun_size (the disc/glow term additive to the base sky colour) and cloud_sun_gain (the cloud rim highlight) are, like every value in this comment, never set by ANY time-of-day preset in this file, so none of the three ever faded with the hour -- energy and yaw moved, the disc's own size and brightness did not. A first attempt trimmed sun_size 0.022 -> 0.016 (~27%) and read as NO visible change; that measured a real property of the shader, not a dead end -- the disc's edges sit at `smoothstep(1-sun_size, 1-sun_size*0.35, sun_dot)`, and near sun_dot=1 the angular radius scales roughly with sqrt(sun_size), so a 27% cut in the raw value is only a ~15% cut in the size actually on screen: far too small to see. A second (scratch, not committed) test at sun_size=0.001/sun_glow=0/cloud_sun_gain=0 confirmed this: the blob shrank to a small, clean, moon-sized disc, proving the mechanism right and only the earlier magnitude wrong. Landed short of fully off, at a size worth actually seeing as a small moon rather than nothing, and re-verified at these exact numbers on the flagged frame (outward-dusk, hour 21): a modest pale disc with a soft, contained glow, no dominant bright mass. cloud_lit/cloud_shade (the cloud's own lit-face colour, independent of the rim highlight and also never time-of-day-driven, default near-white) dimmed and cooled the same way as a secondary, complementary fix -- confirmed on its own it did NOT meaningfully shrink the blob, but sun-facing clouds now read as dim and cool rather than lit-white regardless.
sky._comment_moon_disc_t1_hall_4: T1-HALL-4, 2026-08-30, JUDGE-6 defect 11: the night body "is a soft blurry ellipse with no disc edge -- it reads as a lens bloom rather than an object", measured at ~140px across in `H-03-ramp-foot-night`. Two numbers, one object. `sun_size` 0.006 -> 0.0024 takes the body from roughly 6.3 degrees of angular radius to 4.0 -- still far larger than a real moon, deliberately, because this is a stylised night sky and a physically-sized moon would be a few pixels -- and `sun_disc_edge` 0.35 -> 0.93 is what actually makes it a disc: the falloff now occupies the outer 7% of the radius instead of the outer 65%, so the body has a rim. The glow term is untouched and still surrounds it, which is what stops a hard disc reading as a sticker. Applied to `dawn` as well as `night` -- dawn shares this whole sky block verbatim, and a moon that changes shape between two presets that are otherwise identical would be a new defect. Day and golden did NOT set `sun_disc_edge` at the time and so kept the shader default (0.35): golden hour wants its sun to bloom, and this is not a change to it. UPDATE, VP1 sky retune round 1: day NOW sets its own `sun_disc_edge` (0.75, see the base sky block's `_comment_sun_disc_edge_vp1`) to fix a 'huge soft blob' complaint on the midday sun specifically -- golden and dawn still deliberately leave it unset for the bloom reason above.

dawn._comment_t1_night: T1-NIGHT. Judge 2 measured ground luma climbing monotonically from 22:00 to 02:00 (51 -> 53 -> 56 -> 78 on its scale, confirmed independently here at 53 -> 61 -> 63 -> 85) instead of holding at night's own darkest, moodiest tuning -- the 02:00 frame read as a flat pale-mint wash brighter than golden hour, with moonlight from nowhere and no shadow direction. Root cause: before this entry, `times` had exactly three keyframes (day@8, golden@18, night@0), so the ONLY bracket covering the entire night@0 -> day@8 stretch was one continuous 8-hour linear blend -- the ramp toward day's much brighter numbers started the instant the clock passed midnight, and by 02:00 (t=0.25 of that span) a quarter of the whole night-to-day brightness/colour/desaturation swing had already landed, two hours after the darkest keyframe and three hours before dark_to_hour even says the world should start counting as not-dark. This is not a blend-math bug (T1-SKY already confirmed the blend itself is correct once upstream config is) -- it is a missing keyframe. `dawn` is a straight hold of every night sun/sky/environment value, placed exactly at dark_to_hour (5.0) so the game's own is_dark() boundary and the visual's own boundary now agree: night@0 -> dawn@5 interpolates between two identical dicts, so ground/sky luma cannot move at all across the whole dead-of-night stretch this judge flagged (the 22:00 frame this brief explicitly protects sits in the untouched golden->night span and is unaffected), and the real sunrise brightening now happens once, over dawn@5 -> day@8's 3-hour span, instead of being smeared thinly across 8 hours starting at the wrong end of the night. Every value below is copied verbatim from the night preset above; see that block's own comments (NIGHT-LIGHT, VIS-WORLD, T1-LIGHT) for why each number is what it is. TUNABLE only insofar as night's own values are -- change night, then re-copy here, rather than tuning the two independently and letting them drift apart.

villager_smith._comment: R7.2, moved off the trainer's rig by NP5 (owner directive 2026-08-12). Now NP4-rig's villager_female base, same as villager_farmer's -- the two share a body but keep their own distinct tints, the way villager_keeper and villager_ranger already shared the trainer's rig before this item. NP6: the original #3f5a8c (value 0.55, luminance 0.35) read as a flat black silhouette in outdoor sun once NP2's fix made emission correctly reflect the tint -- both albedo AND the self-lit emission pass darken together now, and a source texture with mid/dark regions multiplied by this tint crushed to near-black. A first fix at the same saturation, value 0.72 (luminance 0.45), still rendered as an unlit silhouette in a real frame (round 1 of this item's blind pass) -- blue is the lowest-weighted channel in perceived luminance (Rec709 ~7%), so a saturated blue needs a much higher raw value than an equal-luminance warm tint before it stops reading dark, and a warm sun contributes little light back onto a blue-heavy albedo. Desaturated (0.55 -> 0.35) and brightened further (value 0.72 -> 0.88, luminance 0.67, matching villager_ranger's) genuinely stopped it reading as a black silhouette (round 2's blind pass), but it was still the visibly weakest of the cast -- the critic traced it to the face specifically, reading as 'pale grey-white... closer to unlit clay than skin'. Desaturated further (0.35 -> 0.18) at the same high value so the multiply stops fighting the skin tone while the hue still reads as a pale chambray/steel-blue distinct from the cast's warmer colours.
